concept_html:
Copy-on-Write (CoW) is always on in pandas 3.0. Every indexing result, such as df[cols], df[mask] or df["a"], behaves as a separate object. Changing it never changes df. pandas copies data only when you write to a shared object, so reads stay cheap.

One consequence: chained assignment never works.

df[df["age"] < 18]["weight"] = 0       # df unchanged, ChainedAssignmentError warning
df.loc[df["age"] < 18, "weight"] = 0   # one step: df changed

The first line writes to a temporary copy, which Python then discards. pandas 3 emits a ChainedAssignmentError warning, but the code keeps running. SettingWithCopyWarning no longer exists.

CoW rewards a second habit: method chaining. Build the result as one expression of steps that each return a new frame.

result = (
    raw
    .rename(columns=COLUMN_MAP)
    .loc[lambda d: d["age"] >= 18]
    .assign(weight=lambda d: d["weight"].clip(upper=5.0))
    .pipe(add_age_band, bins=BINS, labels=LABELS)
)
  • assign(col=lambda d: ...) refers to the frame at that step, not the original raw.
  • .loc[lambda d: ...] filters on the current step.
  • .pipe(func, **kwargs) calls your own pure function (lesson B2-L1) inside the chain.

Chains read top to bottom, leave no half-finished variables (df2, df_tmp, df_final) in the namespace, and do not mutate the input. Keep each chain to about ten steps. Split longer ones into named functions and join them with pipe.

To debug a chain, comment out steps from the bottom up, or add .pipe(lambda d: print(d.shape) or d) between steps.

lines: import pandas as pd
def prepare(raw: pd.DataFrame, column_map: dict[str, str], bins: list[int], labels: list[str]) -> pd.DataFrame:
"""Rename, keep adults, cap weights at 5 and add age bands."""
return (
raw
.rename(columns=column_map)
.loc[lambda d: d["age"] >= 18]
.assign(weight=lambda d: d["weight"].clip(upper=5.0))
.pipe(add_age_band, bins=bins, labels=labels)
)

solution_lines: import pandas as pd
def cap_weights(df: pd.DataFrame, cap: float) -> pd.DataFrame:
"""Keep adults and cap their weights at cap."""
return df.loc[lambda d: d["age"] >= 18].assign(
weight=lambda d: d["weight"].clip(upper=cap)

title: Method chaining and Copy-on-Write
why_html:
An analyst caps extreme weights with df[df["weight"] > 5]["weight"] = 5. On pandas 2 it printed a SettingWithCopyWarning that everyone had learned to ignore. The weights were never capped. Three respondents with weights above 12 moved the reported brand share by 4 points. After the upgrade to pandas 3 the assignment still does nothing, with a different warning.

df.assign(weight=df["weight"].clip(upper=5.0)) or a single df.loc[mask, "weight"] = 5 does what the analyst meant.
